analysis.one_liner: Caps interest rates on consumer loans, including credit cards and payday loans, at 36%.
analysis.headline: The bill to cap consumer interest rates at 36% never left the Senate Banking Committee and expired without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill applies the interest-rate protections already given to military service members under the Military Lending Act to everyone. It caps the interest rate on most consumer credit at 36% per year, blocks regulators from granting exemptions, and lets state attorneys general enforce the cap in court. Home mortgages, car purchase loans, and loans from federal credit unions are excluded. It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee in December 2023 and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who pay high rates on credit cards, payday loans, installment loans, and overdraft-style credit. Under current law, service members get a 36% cap; this would extend the same protection to all consumers, with the same penalties and no exemptions granted by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the Military Lending Act's 36% interest rate cap and related protections from service members and their dependents to all consumers.
Disallows CFPB exemption authority for this cap, so the limit could not be waived case by case.
Allows state attorneys general and state regulators to enforce the cap for three years after a violation, on top of federal remedies.
Requires the CFPB, in consultation with the Defense Department, to issue implementing rules within one year of enactment, consistent with existing military lending rules.

analysis.who_pays: Payday, installment, and other lenders whose business model depends on rates above 36%, and credit card issuers charging the highest rates. Some borrowers with poor credit may find fewer lenders willing to serve them at all if lenders cannot price for the risk.

drawbacks.text: The cap excludes home mortgages, car purchase loans secured by the vehicle, and federal credit union loans, so some of the largest forms of consumer debt remain outside the 36% limit.

A hard 36% cap means lenders who would otherwise charge more for very high-risk borrowers may simply decline to lend, which could cut some low-income borrowers off from emergency credit entirely, a tradeoff researchers have flagged with similar military-style rate caps.
The bill would take effect only after CFPB rules or, at latest, 18 months after enactment, so the relief would be delayed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Extending the existing military cap to everyone is a straightforward consumer protection, and the military version has operated for years. The real tradeoff is access: capping rates protects people from debts that pile up at 100%+ APR, but some borrowers who currently get loans at those rates would be turned away instead. The mortgage and car-loan carve-outs limit the benefit for the debts where people carry the largest balances.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Jack Reed introduced the bill on December 14, 2023, joined by 17 Democratic cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, which held no hearings or markups and never reported it back.
No further action was taken on the bill for the rest of the 118th Congress, which ended January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday and other high-interest consumer lenders, and credit card issuers charging rates near or above 36%, kept their existing market because the bill never advanced. Borrowers paying those rates remain unprotected by any federal cap.

for.name: Jack Reed
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the Senate.

for.name: 17 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Merkley, Brown, Blumenthal, and Booker.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die at referral.

against.name: Payday and high-cost installment lenders
against.what_they_did: A national 36% cap would eliminate most of their lending business; such lenders have long opposed federal rate caps like this one.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and it received no floor action in either chamber.

industries.industry: Payday, title, and high-cost installment lenders
industries.note: These lenders' core business is charging rates far above 36%; the cap would make that illegal for all consumers, as it already is for loans to service members. They profit from rollovers and fees that the cap and its Military Lending Act rules would block.

Most card APRs fall below 36%, so the cap mainly binds for subprime borrowers and card-linked fees and add-on products, which the bill counts toward the finance charge in some cases. Issuers would lose their highest-margin customers and products.
Loans by federal credit unions are carved out of the cap, leaving them under their existing NCUA rate limits rather than the new 36% rule.
